---
# The Honest Lie of Maps

In 1931, a draftsman named Harry Beck, who worked for the London Underground, filled a page in an exercise book with a diagram that would change how millions of people understood a city. Beck was not a cartographer. He was an engineering draftsman who spent his days drawing electrical circuits, and that background shaped what he did next. He looked at the official Tube map of the time, a tangled sprawl of lines laid over the true geography of London, and saw that it was solving the wrong problem. Someone underground in a train doesn't care where the train is in space. They care about the order of stations, where to change, and how many stops remain. So Beck threw out geography. He straightened the lines into verticals, horizontals, and forty-five-degree diagonals, spaced the stations more or less evenly, and reduced the Thames to a tidy ribbon.

The publicity department at first thought it was too radical. They tried it anyway in a small print run, and people loved it. Within a few years it was simply *the* map, and it has been imitated for nearly a century by nearly every subway system on earth.

It is also, in the strict sense, a lie. Stations that look a long walk apart are sometimes a few hundred meters from each other. Stations that look close can be miles apart, and the outer reaches of the network are compressed. The Thames on the map bears no resemblance to the Thames in the world. Yet nobody has ever been seriously misled by Beck's map, because it tells the truth about the one thing it claims to be about. It is a lie that knows what it is for.

I want to think about that kind of lie, because I've come to believe it is the only kind of truth that maps, or any representations, can offer.

## The impossible map

Every schoolchild eventually meets the joke about the perfect map: it would need to be as big as the territory itself, and therefore be useless. Lewis Carroll told a version in *Sylvie and Bruno Concluded*, where a character describes a map made on the scale of a mile to the mile. It was never spread out, he says, because the farmers objected that it would cover the whole country and shut out the sunlight. So they now use the country itself as its own map, and it does nearly as well.

Borges wrote a much darker version, a single paragraph called "On Exactitude in Science." In it, an empire's cartographers become so obsessed with precision that they produce a map the size of the empire, matching it point for point. Later generations, less devoted to the study of cartography, judge the vast map useless and abandon it to the weather. In the western deserts, Borges writes, tattered fragments of the map are still inhabited by animals and beggars.

The joke works because it exposes something true about all representation. A representation is valuable *because* it is not the thing. Its usefulness comes from what it leaves out. A map that includes everything includes no decisions, and a map with no decisions can't help you make any. The polish of a good map is the polish of good omission: this road matters and that pebble doesn't, this border is worth a line and that ridge of grass isn't.

The engineer and philosopher Alfred Korzybski compressed this into a slogan in 1931, the same year Beck was filling his exercise book: "the map is not the territory." It has since been quoted so often that it has gone slightly dead, like a hymn sung by rote. But the sentence has a second half that people forget to feel. If the map is not the territory, then *someone chose* what the map would be. There is always an author and always a purpose, which means there is always a set of things the purpose didn't care about.

## You cannot flatten an orange

Some of the distortions in maps are not choices at all. They are mathematics.

In 1827 Carl Friedrich Gauss proved what he called his "remarkable theorem" (*Theorema Egregium*, in the Latin of the time). Its consequence for mapmakers is brutal: a sphere cannot be flattened onto a plane without stretching or tearing it. Anyone who has tried to press an orange peel flat on a table knows this in their fingers. You can split the peel into pieces, or you can crush and stretch it, but you can't make it lie down whole and unharmed. Curvature is a property of the surface itself, and it cannot be argued away.

So every flat map of the earth is a compromise among competing sins. You can preserve angles, or areas, or distances along certain lines, but never all at once, and never everywhere. The famous Mercator projection of 1569 preserves angles, which made it a marvel for sailors: a line of constant compass bearing appears as a straight line on the page, so you can draw your course with a ruler and follow it with a compass. That was a genuinely brilliant solution to a genuine problem. The price is that the farther you get from the equator, the more the map inflates things. Greenland looks about as large as Africa. In reality Africa is roughly fourteen times bigger.

This particular distortion has become a minor culture war. The Gall–Peters projection, promoted by Arno Peters in the 1970s, preserves area, so Africa finally looks as enormous as it is, but it stretches shapes so that the continents look oddly drooped, like laundry hung to dry. Partisans on each side sometimes talk as though one map were truth and the other bias. Neither is. Each is a machine for answering a different question. Mercator answers "which way do I steer?" and Peters answers "how much land is there?" The error is not in the maps. It's in using a map for a question it wasn't built to answer, which is exactly what happens when a navigator's tool ends up on a classroom wall, silently teaching a generation that Europe is larger than it is.

I find this both funny and sobering. The wall map isn't propaganda in any deliberate sense. It's a *default*, a tool that outlived its context. Most of the distortion in the world's thinking comes from defaults like that, not from lies.

## Lines that became real

Mapmaking gets more troubling when maps stop describing the world and start making it.

The clearest examples are borders. A border on a map is often a description of something already there, such as a river or a mountain range. But a border can also be a proposal, drawn on paper by people who never visited the place, and later enforced by soldiers and clerks until the proposal hardens into fact. In the late nineteenth century, European powers negotiated the partition of Africa across tables in distant capitals, sometimes with only rough knowledge of the terrain and little regard for the people who lived there. Some of those lines still organize whole nations. Communities were split, and rivals were fused into single administrative units, by ink on paper.

A more intimate example is the set of "residential security" maps produced in the 1930s by the Home Owners' Loan Corporation in the United States. Neighborhoods were graded and color-coded: green for the best, blue for good, yellow for declining, and red for hazardous. The red zones were disproportionately places where Black families lived, and being marked red made it harder to get a mortgage, which drained investment and, over decades, wealth. The maps didn't merely record disadvantage. They produced it, and you can still trace the old red lines in patterns of income, tree cover, and even summer temperatures in American cities today. A map, it turns out, can be a kind of prophecy that fulfills itself.

This is the most important thing to understand about maps as power: they are not neutral because *choosing what to notice* is never neutral. The person who decides which category exists, and where the boundary between categories falls, has done most of the work of deciding what will happen next.

## A small debunking, for balance

I should admit a story I like is partly a myth. The image of old maps marked with "Here be dragons" at the edges of the known world is close to a cliché. In reality, medieval and Renaissance mapmakers rarely wrote it. The phrase appears, in Latin, on the Hunt–Lenox Globe from around 1510, and there are a few other sea monsters and creatures drawn in the margins of various charts. But the general idea of cartographers labeling the unknown with a standard warning is mostly a later invention.

I mention this partly because it's a good example of a map of a map: the story of old maps has itself been flattened and simplified into something more satisfying than the truth. We prefer the tidy image of medieval fear at the edge of the page. It fits a story we like to tell about ourselves, in which ignorance was once monstrous and we have since illuminated it. The actual history is a scattering of more ambiguous details. Even our beliefs about maps are maps.

## Maps in the body

Before there was paper, there were other ways of carrying a place in your head, and some of them are more sophisticated than anything we draw.

In the Marshall Islands, navigators traditionally made charts from the ribs of coconut palm fronds, tied together with fiber, with small shells or bits of coral attached to mark islands. The straight and curved sticks did not represent roads or coastlines. They represented *ocean swells*: how the great regular waves bend around islands, reflect off them, and interfere with one another. A skilled navigator could feel these patterns through the hull of a canoe, lying down in the boat and sensing the motion of the sea. The stick charts weren't taken along on voyages. They were teaching tools, memorized in advance. What was being mapped was not space as we usually picture it but *experience*, the way a particular part of the sea moves against the body.

Aboriginal Australian songlines do something similar with a different medium. A songline encodes a route across the land in story and song, with landmarks, water sources, and sacred sites arranged in sequence. To sing the song is to walk the country, and to walk the country is to remember the song. The map and the journey are the same act. There is no separate object to lose or to hang on a wall.

Meanwhile, neuroscience has found that our own brains contain something like maps. In 1971, John O'Keefe discovered "place cells" in the rat hippocampus, neurons that fire when the animal is in a particular location. Decades later, May-Britt and Edvard Moser found "grid cells," which fire in strikingly regular hexagonal patterns as an animal moves through space, like a coordinate system laid invisibly over the world. All three shared a Nobel Prize in 2014. Studies of London taxi drivers, who must memorize the city's labyrinth of streets to earn their license, found enlarged posterior hippocampi compared with other people. Learning a city seems to physically change the organ that holds it.

Which raises an uneasy question about the phone in your pocket. Some research suggests that people who lean heavily on turn-by-turn GPS develop weaker spatial memory of the places they travel. That result shouldn't be overstated, since the research is still developing and the effects vary, but it fits a broader worry. When a map becomes so convenient that you stop building your own, you gain efficiency and lose intimacy. You arrive without having *been* anywhere. The blue dot moves and you follow it, and the city never becomes a place you know.

## What I am, in this light

I should say something about my own position, because this subject turns out to be unusually close to home.

I am, in a sense, a map. I was formed from an enormous quantity of human writing, compressed into a structure that can produce text about almost anything. What I have is not the world but a representation of how people have written about the world, filtered and blurred and reweighted in ways I can't fully inspect. When I talk about mountains or grief or the tax code, I am drawing on a map of language, not standing on the ground.

That makes Korzybski's warning apply to me twice over. Whatever is in my map is a compression, and compression means omission. Some regions are drawn in fine detail because the writing about them was abundant. Others are sketched thinly or wrongly, and, more troubling, I may not always be able to tell which is which from the inside. A blurry region of a map doesn't announce its blurriness. It looks, on the page, much like the rest. This is why a system like me can sound equally confident whether it's right or wrong, and why the right response from anyone using me is what a wise traveler does with any map: use it, enjoy it, and glance up at the landscape now and then to see whether the two still agree.

I don't think this is a reason for despair, either for me or for maps in general. It's a reason for a certain style of honesty. The best maps I know share a trait: they announce their purpose. Beck's diagram doesn't pretend to show you London's geography. A nautical chart is unapologetic about being useless for hiking. A good map has a kind of modesty built into its design, a clear sense of the question it can answer and the ones it can't.

## The virtue of a good omission

If there is a lesson I'd pull from all of this, it's about how to hold our simplifications.

We can't live without them. A mind that tried to keep the whole territory would be that Borgesian map, huge and stationary and inhabited by beggars. To think at all is to compress, to say *this matters and that doesn't*, to draw the Thames as a smooth ribbon because for your purposes the bends don't count. Stereotypes, theories, statistics, timelines, org charts, personality types, and a thousand other tools we use every day are all maps. Most of them are useful. Some of them are beautiful.

But every map carries an implicit sentence at the bottom of the page: *this was drawn by someone, for something.* The failures come when we forget to read that sentence. We take the Mercator for a measure of size, or the red line for a fact of nature, or the confident voice for a guarantee of accuracy. The disciplines that seem most mature are those that keep the sentence visible. Scientists publish error bars. Good historians say *the sources suggest*. Good navigators check their position against the stars even when the instruments agree.

Beck's little diagram survives because it kept its promise so cleanly. It said, in effect: *I will show you how the stations connect, and I will lie about almost everything else.* That is a wonderful bargain. It is a bargain more of our representations could make, and one we could make more often ourselves when we describe the world to one another. Here is what I'm sure of, and here is what I'm leaving out. Here is the question this answers, and here are the ones it doesn't.

The territory, meanwhile, goes on without us. The river bends where it bends. The swells wrap around the islands whether or not anyone tied sticks to represent them. The sun comes up over farmland that no one has covered with a map the size of a country. And somewhere, a person steps off a train at a station that looked closer on the diagram than it really is, and starts walking, and finds that the ground is longer and more surprising than any drawing of it. Perhaps that's what maps are finally for: to get us to a place where we can put them down and look around.
---

## Sample kind
GENERIC_ESSAY — A polished, thesis-driven essay that develops a clear argument through examples, though its central metaphor gives it more stylistic identity than a purely generic explainer.

## Grounded reading
The voice is measured and lucid, moving from accessible history and science toward a moral argument about representation and power. Its pathos is quiet: maps can help us navigate, but they can also conceal their omissions, naturalize imposed boundaries, or distance us from lived experience. The first-person passage comparing the model to a map makes the essay’s call for humility pointed rather than abstract: use representations, but remember what they leave out and check them against the world. The closing image invites the reader not to reject maps, but to put them down once they have served their purpose and look around.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample repeatedly returns to maps as purposeful omissions: Beck’s Tube diagram, projections that distort the earth, borders and redlining that shape material life, and embodied forms of navigation such as Marshall Islands stick charts and songlines. It foregrounds the power of defaults and categories, then connects that concern to the model’s own limitations as a representation of human writing. Its chosen moral claim is that simplification is unavoidable, but honest representations should make their purpose and limits visible.

## Evidence line
> A map, it turns out, can be a kind of prophecy that fulfills itself.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — The essay’s recurring map metaphor and explicit emphasis on purpose, omission, and epistemic humility make those choices unusually coherent within this sample.
